## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.64478.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.64478.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

Your fluorescent bead technology enables the characterization of specific metabolic features within the gut microbiome. The new methodology has allowed you to begin to explore biochemical activities of gut microbiota in situ. We view this as an important step forward in the area of microbiome research.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for sending your article entitled "Microbiota functional activity biosensors for characterizing nutrient utilization in vivo" for peer review at eLife. Your article has been evaluated by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Wendy Garrett as the Senior Editor.

There was enthusiasm for acceptance of your work but some concern about focus. The reviewers are quite interested about the fluorogenic bead technology and its application for microbiome studies. They have made recommendations about how you might strengthen the connection between the results describing how Bacteroides degrade these fibers and the technology. Consensus of the reviewers is that this is a manuscript about a powerful tool and its application rather than a deep dive into the underlying biology. If you can recast the work in light of the reviewers' comments and concerns and modify the text so that it is more conservative it its claims, we are of the opinion that it would be quite appropriate for publication in eLife. The reviewers express a desire to add some minor additional supporting data for some of your experiments (for example as regards Figure 5D). We are providing reviewer comments but to clarify are not asking for extensive new experimentation.

Reviewer #1

I agree with the conclusions the authors draw from the enumeration, INSeq, and proteomic measurements presented in Figure 2 (and its supplements) and Figure 5 - in short, that specific PULs harbored by strains in the synthetic community determine the degree of glycan degradation observed on the beads recovered from mice. It might be nice to run a confirmatory experiment with, e.g., a community in which wild-type BT is replaced by a δ-PUL7 or δ-PUL75 mutant, but the data are already convincing in their current form.

Likely outside the scope of this manuscript, but are the authors able to isolate bacterial cells or genetic material from beads recovered from a mouse? One could imagine an anchor organism that consumes the fiber or simply uses it as a physical niche. Might be especially interesting if bead-associated communities had structure and could be imaged using FISH.

Reviewer #2:

Wesener and colleagues present a method for characterizing biochemical activities of gut microbes in vivo. First, the authors purified and extensively characterized a polysaccharide fraction rich in arabinan (PFABN) and compared the biological activity of PFABN to that of unfractionated pea fiber and arabinan purified from sugar beet (SBABN) using in vitro growth assays/substrate degradation using monocultures of several Bacteroides species, establishing the impact of these on bacterial metabolism. They also characterized responses to these fibers in vivo, in mice colonized with a synthetic community composed of 14 species, consuming diet with/without these fibers. Authors used community-wide proteomic measurements and transposon mutant analyses (TnSeq) for five Bacteroides species to investigate genes involved in the utilization of these fibers and genes important for fitness in these fibers for the 5 Bacteroides species. In the second half of the paper the authors describe methods for generating “Microbiota Functional Activity Biosensors” (MFABs), which consist of glycans covalently-linked to the surface of fluorescent paramagnetic microscopic glass beads. They characterize MFABs and perform validation studies (i.e., quantification of glycan metabolism) in vitro and in gnotobiotic mice. Using unique fluorogenic tags authors analyze simultaneously multiple bead types with different immobilized polysaccharides. Presented results suggest that colocalizing different polysaccharides on the bead surface can have a synergistic effect on their degradation modulated by diet. These newly developed Microbiota Functional Activity Biosensors are a significant contribution to the field as options for measuring gut microbiota biochemical activities in vivo are currently very limited. Also, the study contributes valuable datasets on bacterial (proteomics/InSeq for 5 Bacteroides species) that will be useful to other scientists studying the microbiome. Specific comments:

The paper comes across as having two major parts that could be better integrated. Testing whether any of the key PULs identified for degradation of PFABN/SBABN (results from INSeq/proteomics) impact degradation of these fibers in the beads in vitro (or vivo) would strengthen the connection between the results describing how Bacteroides degrade these fibers and the new development.

Not clear how the statistical differences in growth were determined in Figure 1. i.e., what values were used? Growth rate during exponential phase? Should be indicated.

Bead assays: What fraction of the beads orally-gavaged are recovered from the mice? Also, in the Materials and methods authors mention that beads were collected from cecum and/or from fecal pellets. Does collection site affect the extent to which glycans on the beads are metabolized?

Beads assays ii. The measurement of glycans that remain bound to the beads informs what it is released from them. It is likely that in the context of a complex community most/all? of the released carbohydrates are also used by microbes. This may not always be true, particularly in monocultures or in experiments in mice with small communities. This should be discussed.

"The results disclosed that the fitness scores of 332, 195, and 75 genes were significantly altered during diet supplementation with pea fiber, PFABN, or SBABN, respectively (Supplementary file 4) (adjusted p-value < 0.05, FDR-corrected)" Not clear what species is being discussed here. Supplementary file 4 contains 12 tables (3 supplemented substrates/4 Bacteroides strains).

Reviewer #3:

This manuscript represents a technical tour de force, and describes an approach to trace and understand metabolic pathways generated by single compounds in a complex ecosystem such as the mouse gut. An outstanding research team has applied many state of the art methodologies to examine the effects of particular dietary substrates on bacterial growth and gene expression. This represents a technological advance but the extent of the advance is not clear, since the results often are marginal. Although a great deal of work has been performed, the overall significance of the work is not obvious.

Several specific points should be addressed as well:

The pea fiber arabinan is only 71% of the purified polysaccharide. What is the significance of the substantial carbohydrate contamination? Can it really be called purified with such extensive contamination? The results in Figure 4 indicate that the xylan component materially affects the results.

What is is the significance of the long lag phase for B. ovatus with glucose as the substrate? That pattern is unlike all other conditions.

Figure 2. Panels B and C seem to be contradictory. All of the indicated bacteria grew as well on PF as on the “purified” polysaccharides in panels B (and in all cases grew better than on PFABN, but a marked difference is shown in panel C. This is difficult to reconcile.

Figure 2—figure supplement 2. Not surprisingly, results for PF and PFABN were similar, but they were not very different from SBABN. It is difficult to understand what actually was shown here. Although elegant, it is unclear what the fitness calculations add to the calculations of protein abundance. Almost all of the significant variance is along the axis of the protein abundances. A considerable number of the data points for the specified proteins are above the zero line for fitness. (mutant grew better than wild-type). The authors should account for the fitness variation in both directions, and not just cherry-pick the ones that support their hypothesis.

Figure 3C. Why are the results shown for SBABN when he main thrust of the paper is PFABN? If the method is universal, then the PFABN results should be similar.

Figure 4. Panel B is confusing-are the germ-free mice shown under the heading colonized? That is the only way to reconcile the text and figure. But then why are sugars metabolized in the GF animals? Or are the GF mice not shown? This point needs to be clarified since it affects the interpretation of the results.

Figure 5 panel D. The y-axis in the two sub-panels that deal with the glucomannan coated beads are different. In the HISF/LoFV columns, the results of the 2 conditions differ, but the pea fiber results are the same across the panels-this difference is the source of the author's claims, but this seems in the realm of experimental variation, rather than biological meaning. There should be more confirmation of the points that the authors are making, since they end with a strong statement of impact without the necessary rigor.

Discussion: In general, the Discussion overstates the significance of the actual findings. The broad statements should be toned down. The limitations of the purification methods should be acknowledged and how that affects the results achieved should be addressed.

claims.source: Three MFABs, each containing a unique glycan/fluorophore combination, were simultaneously orally gavaged into gnotobiotic mice, recovered from their intestines, and analyzed to directly quantify bacterial metabolism of structurally distinct arabinans in different human diet contexts.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data on polysaccharide degradation from recovered beads under different dietary conditions.

claims.claim: Colocalizing pea-fiber arabinan and glucomannan on the bead surface enhanced in vivo degradation of glucomannan.
claims.source: Colocalizing pea-fiber arabinan and another polysaccharide (glucomannan) on the bead surface enhanced in vivo degradation of glucomannan.
claims.evidence: Figure 5D shows significantly more glucomannan was degraded when colocalized with PFABN on beads in mice receiving pea fiber-supplemented diet compared to glucomannan alone.

claims.claim: The gut microbiota is complex and dynamic and exhibits considerable intra- and interpersonal variation in its configurations.
claims.source: The gut microbiota is complex and dynamic and exhibits considerable intra- and interpersonal variation in its configurations (Lloyd-Price et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lloyd-Price et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Methods of food processing affect the representation of bioactive food components.
claims.source: Furthermore, much needs to be learned about the effects of current methods of food processing on the representation of bioactive food components (Carmody et al., 2015; Wolf et al., 2019), and about the mechanisms that determine whether and how microbes compete and/or cooperate for them.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carmody et al., 2015 and Wolf et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Plant fibers are complex mixtures of biomolecules whose composition varies depending upon their source, method of initial recovery, and the food processing techniques used.
claims.source: Plant fibers are complex mixtures of biomolecules whose composition varies depending upon their source, method of initial recovery, and the food processing techniques used to incorporate them into food products that have satisfactory organoleptic properties (texture, taste, smell) (Shahidi and Ho, 1998; Caffall and Mohnen, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shahidi and Ho, 1998 and Caffall and Mohnen, 2009.

claims.claim: Plant fibers are composed of but not limited to polysaccharides, proteins, fatty acids, polyphenols, and other plant-derived small molecules.
claims.source: Plant fibers are composed of but not limited to polysaccharides, proteins, fatty acids, polyphenols, and other plant-derived small molecules (Nicholson et al., 2012; Scalbert et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nicholson et al., 2012 and Scalbert et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Knowledge of the genetic underpinnings of how various members of the gut microbiota recognize and metabolize glycans has increased substantially in recent years.
claims.source: Nonetheless, knowledge of the genetic underpinnings of how various members of the gut microbiota recognize and metabolize glycans has increased substantially in recent years through a combination of in vitro and in vivo approaches (Brown and Koropatkin, 2020; Kaoutari et al., 2013; Ndeh and Gilbert, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown and Koropatkin, 2020; Kaoutari et al., 2013; and Ndeh and Gilbert, 2018.

claims.claim: Having a suitable complement of genes for acquiring and processing a given glycan structure in vitro does not necessarily predict whether that organism will be a consumer in vivo.
claims.source: Knowing that a given microbiota member has a suitable complement of genes for acquiring and processing a given glycan structure in vitro does not necessarily predict whether that organism will be a consumer in vivo (Flint et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Flint et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Pea fiber was selected based on results obtained from a screen of 34 types of food-grade crude plant fibers.
claims.source: Pea fiber was selected based on results obtained from a screen we conducted of 34 types of food-grade crude plant fibers obtained from various sources, including the byproducts of food manufacturing (Patnode et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patnode et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The screen was performed in gnotobiotic mice colonized with a defined consortium of cultured sequenced human gut bacterial strains, including several saccharolytic Bacteroides species.
claims.source: The screen was performed in gnotobiotic mice colonized with a defined consortium of cultured sequenced human gut bacterial strains, including several saccharolytic Bacteroides species.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the referenced screening study.

claims.claim: Supplementation of the HiSF-LoFV diet with fiber generated from the seed coat of the pea, Pisum sativum, produced a significant increase in the abundance of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron.
claims.source: Supplementation of this 'HiSF-LoFV' diet with fiber generated from the seed coat of the pea, Pisum sativum, produced a significant increase in the abundance of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (Patnode et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patnode et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The isolated pea fiber fraction (fraction 8; 4M KOH) possessed high carbohydrate and low protein content, high monosaccharide diversity, and a high relative proportion of arabinose.
claims.source: The fraction isolated under the harshest conditions (fraction 8; 4M KOH) possessed high carbohydrate and low protein content, high monosaccharide diversity, and a high relative proportion of arabinose.
claims.evidence: This is based on analytical characterization data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The mole percent representation of arabinose in the isolated pea fiber arabinan was 71%.
claims.source: The mole percent representation of arabinose in the end product was 71% (corresponding values for xylose, galactose, and glucose were 12%, 11% and 6%, respectively) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of monosaccharide composition shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Glycosyl-linkage analysis of the isolated glycan revealed a 2-O-branched arabinan attached to small rhamnogalacturonan-I (RGI) pectic fragments and small galactan oligomers.
claims.source: Glycosyl-linkage analysis of the isolated glycan revealed a 2-O-branched arabinan (5-substituted arabinose, 2,5-substituted arabinose, 2,3,5-substituted arabinose) (Figure 1B) attached to small rhamnogalacturonan-I (RGI) pectic fragments (2-substituted and 2,4-substituted rhamnose) and small galactan oligomers (4-substituted galactose) (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on glycosyl-linkage analysis data presented in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Approximately 90% of all non-starch carbohydrate in PFABN is represented by what is likely a single species of polysaccharide, with the remaining being xylan.
claims.source: We named the isolated polysaccharide fraction 'pea fiber arabinan' (PFABN) based on (1) these linkage results, (2) the fact that arabinose comprises the majority of its monosaccharide content (71 mole percent), and (3) our observation that ~90% of all non-starch carbohydrate is represented by what is likely a single species of polysaccharide, with the remaining being xylan.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' analysis of the linkage and monosaccharide composition data.

claims.claim: Sugar beet arabinan (SBABN) is primarily 3-O-branched.
claims.source: Unlike PFABN, sugar beet arabinan (SBABN) is primarily 3-O-branched as revealed by glycosyl-linkage analysis (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on glycosyl-linkage analysis data presented in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: PFABN contains twofold more triply branched 2,3,5-substituted arabinose monomers than SBABN.
claims.source: PFABN also contains twofold more triply branched 2,3,5-substituted arabinose monomers, suggesting it is more sterically encumbered than SBABN.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of glycosyl-linkage analysis data for PFABN and SBABN.

claims.claim: PFABN is more sterically encumbered than SBABN.
claims.source: PFABN also contains twofold more triply branched 2,3,5-substituted arabinose monomers, suggesting it is more sterically encumbered than SBABN.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the higher content of triply branched arabinose monomers in PFABN.

claims.claim: B. ovatus ATCC 8483, B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 grew on isolated PFABN and SBABN, although less rapidly during the exponential phase of growth and to a lower cell density than in medium containing an equivalent concentration of d-glucose.
claims.source: In vitro assays performed in a minimal defined medium (McNulty et al., 2013) with Bacteroides type strains established that B. ovatus ATCC 8483, B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 grew on isolated PFABN and SBABN, although less rapidly during the exponential phase of growth and to a lower cell density than in medium containing an equivalent concentration of d-glucose (results based on measurements of OD600; see Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro growth assays shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 grew as rapidly or faster and to the same or higher density on PFABN and SBABN, respectively, compared to d-glucose.
claims.source: In contrast, B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 grew as rapidly or faster and to the same or higher density on PFABN and SBABN, respectively, compared to d-glucose (p<0.05, one-way analysis of variance [ANOVA] with Tukey's honest significant difference, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro growth assays with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 reached exponential growth more quickly on PFABN and SBABN than when d-glucose was present in the medium.
claims.source: B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 also reached exponential growth more quickly than when d-glucose was present in this medium (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro growth assays shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The 14-member consortium contained 58,537 known or predicted protein-coding genes.
claims.source: Adult germ-free C57Bl/6J mice were colonized with a 14-member consortium of sequenced bacterial strains containing 58,537 known or predicted protein-coding genes.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the bacterial strains in the consortium.

claims.claim: Five of the Bacteroides were each represented by previously described libraries of tens of thousands of transposon (Tn) insertion mutants.
claims.source: Five of the Bacteroides (B. thetaiotaomicron strains VPI-5482 and 7330, B. vulgatus ATCC 8482, B. cellulosilyticus WH2, B. ovatus ATCC 8483) were each represented by previously described libraries of tens of thousands of transposon (Tn) insertion mutants (Hibberd et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Hibberd et al., 2017 and Wu et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The overall change in abundance of each mutant library in response to various diet manipulations was similar to the corresponding parental wild-type strain.
claims.source: These studies had shown that collectively the overall change in abundance of each mutant library in response to various diet manipulations was similar to the corresponding parental wild-type strain.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies cited (Hibberd et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2015).

claims.claim: B. thetaiotaomicron 7330 failed to colonize mice at levels above a (relative) abundance of 0.1% under any of the diet conditions tested.
claims.source: Of the 14-member consortium, only B. thetaiotaomicron 7330 failed to colonize mice at levels above a (relative) abundance of 0.1% under any of the diet conditions tested.
claims.evidence: This is based on community profiling data from the experiments.

claims.claim: B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 responded to all three supplements (pea fiber, PFABN, and SBABN).
claims.source: Five community members exhibited statistically significant, albeit distinct, differences in their absolute abundances in response to specific glycan preparations: (1) B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 responded to all three supplements
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of community profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: B. ovatus ATCC 8483 increased after exposure to both intact pea fiber and PFABN but not to SBABN.
claims.source: (2) B. ovatus ATCC 8483 increased after exposure to both intact pea fiber and PFABN but not to SBABN
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of community profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 exhibited significant increases with SBABN.
claims.source: (3) B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 exhibited significant increases with SBABN
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of community profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: B. cellulosilyticus WH2 and Ruminococcaceae sp. TSDC 17.2 increased significantly when exposed to intact pea fiber but not to either of the isolated arabinan preparations.
claims.source: (4) B. cellulosilyticus WH2 and Ruminococcaceae sp. TSDC 17.2 increased significantly when exposed to intact pea fiber but not to either of the isolated arabinan preparations (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2) (p<0.01, generalized linear mixed-effects model [Gaussian]; two-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of community profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Both isolated arabinan preparations had a significantly greater specific activity compared to intact pea fiber at the doses tested.
claims.source: This metric of specific activity, which takes into account the absolute mass of supplement consumed daily by members of the different groups of mice, revealed that both of the isolated arabinan preparations had a significantly greater effect compared to intact pea fiber at the doses tested (Figure 2C) (p<0.05 mixed-effects linear model [Gaussian]; one-way ANOVA with Tukey's honest significant difference, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of specific activity data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Bacteroides spp. possess multiple polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs).
claims.source: Bacteroides spp. possess multiple polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs); a shared feature of PULs is an adjacent pair of susC and susD homologs responsible for binding extracellular polysaccharide fragments and importing them into the periplasm.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Bacteroides species.

claims.claim: A shared feature of PULs is an adjacent pair of susC and susD homologs responsible for binding extracellular polysaccharide fragments and importing them into the periplasm.
claims.source: Bacteroides spp. possess multiple polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs); a shared feature of PULs is an adjacent pair of susC and susD homologs responsible for binding extracellular polysaccharide fragments and importing them into the periplasm.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about PUL structure and function.

claims.claim: PUL genes encode various carbohydrate active enzymes (CAZymes) involved in polysaccharide depolymerization.
claims.source: PUL genes also encode various carbohydrate active enzymes (CAZymes) involved in polysaccharide depolymerization, as well as transcriptional regulators that allow the locus to be induced in the presence of glycans it can recognize/utilize (Anderson and Salyers, 1989; Terrapon et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Salyers, 1989 and Terrapon et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Regulated expression of PULs allows bacteria to acquire nutrients within the highly competitive environment of the gut.
claims.source: Regulated expression of PULs allows bacteria to acquire nutrients within the highly competitive environment of the gut (Martens et al., 2011; Tuncil et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Martens et al., 2011 and Tuncil et al., 2017.

claims.claim: 14, 12, 11, and 8 PULs were identified as responsive to at least one of the diet supplements in B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482, B. ovatus ATCC 8483, B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and B. vulgatus ATCC 8482, respectively.
claims.source: Based on gene set enrichment analysis (Luo et al., 2009), we identified 14, 12, 11, and 8 PULs that we deemed 'responsive' to at least one of the diet supplements in B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 (BT), B. ovatus ATCC 8483 (Bovatus), B. cellulosilyticus WH2 (BcellWH2), and B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 (BVU), respectively (adjusted p-value<0.05, unpaired one-sample Z-test, FDR-corrected).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis of metaproteomic data.

claims.claim: The fitness scores of a total of 39 genes in B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482, 135 genes in B. ovatus ATCC 8483, 346 genes in B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and 82 genes in B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 were significantly decreased during diet supplementation with either pea fiber, PFABN, or SBABN.
claims.source: The results disclosed that the fitness scores of a total of 39 genes in B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482, 135 genes in B. ovatus ATCC 8483, 346 genes in B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and 82 genes in B. vulgatus ATCC 8482 were significantly decreased during diet supplementation with either pea fiber, PFABN, or SBABN (Supplementary file 4) (adjusted p-value<0.05, FDR corrected).
claims.evidence: This is based on INSeq analysis of transposon mutant libraries.

claims.claim: PFABN is a key bioactive component of pea fiber utilized by B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482, B. vulgatus ATCC 8482, B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and B. ovatus ATCC 8483.
claims.source: Together, these community configurational and functional responses to diet supplementation provided evidence that PFABN is a key bioactive component of pea fiber utilized by B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482, B. vulgatus ATCC 8482, B. cellulosilyticus WH2, and B. ovatus ATCC 8483.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined community profiling, metaproteomic, and INSeq data.

claims.claim: Amine plus phosphonate functionalized beads contain 2.18 × 10^10 ± 3.49 × 10^9 reactive amines per bead.
claims.source: The results revealed that amine plus phosphonate functionalized beads contain 2.18 × 1010 ± 3.49 × 109 (mean ± s.d.) reactive amines per bead versus 1.20 × 109 ± 1.92 × 108 reactive amines after surface acetylation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on ninhydrin-based colorimetric assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Streptavidin-coated beads possess 23-fold fewer potential binding sites than amine plus phosphonate functionalized beads.
claims.source: By comparison, streptavidin-coated beads used in our previously published procedure (Patnode et al., 2019) possess 23-fold fewer potential binding sites (9.21 × 108 ± 1.13 × 108 molecules of biotin per bead).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of quantified binding sites between the two bead types.

claims.claim: Incubation with a combination of endo-arabinanase and α-l-arabinofuranosidase enzymes removed 88 ± 1.2% of the immobilized PFABN after 30 min.
claims.source: Incubation with a combination of endo-arabinanase and α-l-arabinofuranosidase enzymes removed 88 ± 1.2% (mean ± s.d.) of the immobilized PFABN after 30 min while incubation with each enzyme individually removed greater than 80% of the glycan after 30 min and more than 90% after 20 hr.
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme degradation assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: An endo-inulinase with specificity toward β(1-2)-linked fructose resides failed to degrade PFABN.
claims.source: In contrast, an endo-inulinase with specificity toward β(1-2)-linked fructose resides failed to degrade PFABN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro enzyme degradation assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Added PFABN was required for degradation of immobilized PFABN from beads by B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 and B. cellulosilyticus WH2 in vitro.
claims.source: Under the conditions tested, added PFABN was required for degradation of immobilized PFABN from beads; the amount of PFABN removed from the bead surface increased with increasing incubation time, with maximum values of 64 ± 9% (mean ± s.d.) and 48 ± 3% achieved with B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 and B. cellulosilyticus WH2, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro bacterial degradation assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The quantities of neutral monosaccharides liberated by acid hydrolysis from the surfaces of beads recovered from the cecums of germ-free mice were not significantly different from the amounts liberated from the input bead preparations with one exception.
claims.source: The quantities of neutral monosaccharides liberated by acid hydrolysis from the surfaces of beads recovered from the cecums of germ-free mice were not significantly different from the amounts liberated from the input bead preparations with one exception – a slight, albeit statistically significant, increase in galactose from beads coated with PFABN and SBABN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; p<0.05, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of beads recovered from germ-free mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The mass of arabinose was significantly decreased when PFABN- or SBABN-coated beads were recovered from colonized mice fed the unsupplemented HiSF-LoFV diet.
claims.source: In contrast to germ-free controls (see Figure 4—figure supplement 3), the mass of arabinose was significantly decreased when PFABN- or SBABN-coated beads were recovered from colonized mice fed the unsupplemented HiSF-LoFV diet (Figure 4B,C; p<0.05, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of beads recovered from colonized mice shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: Supplementation with unfractionated pea fiber induced a community configuration associated with significantly increased capacity to degrade both PFABN and SBABN.
claims.source: Compared to the base HiSF-LoFV diet, supplementation with unfractionated pea fiber induced a community configuration associated with significantly increased capacity to degrade both PFABN and SBABN as judged by the amount of arabinose remaining on recovered beads (Figure 4B,C; p<0.05, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of beads recovered from colonized mice shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: Loss of arabinose from either PFABN- or SBABN-beads was not significantly different between the two bead types when the HiSF-LoFV diet was supplemented with either of these isolated arabinan preparations.
claims.source: Loss of arabinose from either PFABN- or SBABN-beads was not significantly different between the two bead types when the HiSF-LoFV diet was supplemented with either of these isolated arabinan preparations, demonstrating functional equivalence in the capacity of each community to utilize either arabinan (see Figure 4B,C and Supplementary file 5 which provides evidence that results from cecal samples [Experiment 1] and fecal samples [Experiment 2] were comparable).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of bead degradation data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: Xylan was more efficiently processed by the microbiota in all three supplemented diet contexts.
claims.source: Beads coated in PFABN revealed that xylan (xylose monosaccharide remaining on PFABN beads) was more efficiently processed by the microbiota in all three supplemented diet contexts (Figure 4B; p<0.05, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of xylose remaining on beads shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The galactan content from both arabinan preparations was not utilized under any of the diet conditions tested.
claims.source: In contrast to xylan, the galactan content from both arabinan preparations was not utilized under any of the diet conditions tested (Figure 4B,C and Supplementary file 5), suggesting that β(1-4) galactan degradation in vivo has lower priority compared to the available arabinan (Tuncil et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of galactose remaining on beads shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: β(1-4) galactan degradation in vivo has lower priority compared to the available arabinan.
claims.source: In contrast to xylan, the galactan content from both arabinan preparations was not utilized under any of the diet conditions tested (Figure 4B,C and Supplementary file 5), suggesting that β(1-4) galactan degradation in vivo has lower priority compared to the available arabinan (Tuncil et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of galactan degradation and supported by citation to Tuncil et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Among the pea fiber-responsive Bacteroides, only B. ovatus ATCC 8483 and B. cellulosilyticus WH2 were able to grow in minimal medium containing glucomannan as the sole carbon source.
claims.source: We found that among the pea fiber-responsive Bacteroides identified above, only B. ovatus ATCC 8483 and B. cellulosilyticus WH2 were able to grow in minimal medium containing glucomannan as the sole carbon source (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro growth assays shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: B. ovatus ATCC 8483 and B. cellulosilyticus WH2 have PULs known to be induced by glucomannan in vitro.
claims.source: Both organisms have PULs known to be induced by glucomannan in vitro (PUL28 in B. cellulosilyticus WH2; PULs 52 and 80 in B. ovatus ATCC 8483); each of these PULs encodes at least one GH26 enzyme with β-mannanase activity (Bågenholm et al., 2017; Martens et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bågenholm et al., 2017 and Martens et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Glucomannan on beads coated with glucomannan alone was degraded to a similar extent in mice receiving the unsupplemented or pea fiber-supplemented HiSF-LoFV diets.
claims.source: The results revealed that glucomannan on beads coated with glucomannan alone was degraded to a similar extent in mice receiving the unsupplemented or pea fiber-supplemented HiSF-LoFV diets (Figure 5D and Supplementary file 5; p=0.87, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of beads recovered from mice shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: When presented with PFABN on the same bead, significantly more glucomannan was degraded by the microbiota of mice receiving the pea fiber-supplemented diet as compared to the unsupplemented diet.
claims.source: However, when presented with PFABN on the same bead, significantly more glucomannan was degraded by the microbiota of mice receiving the pea fiber-supplemented diet as compared to the unsupplemented diet (Figure 5D; p<0.05, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of beads recovered from mice shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The amount of arabinose remaining on beads coated with PFABN and glucomannan, and PFABN alone, was significantly reduced with pea fiber supplementation.
claims.source: The amount of arabinose remaining on beads coated with PFABN and glucomannan, and PFABN alone, was also significantly reduced (degradation increased) with pea fiber supplementation (Figure 5D; p<0.05, Mann–Whitney U test).
claims.evidence: This is based on GC-MS analysis of beads recovered from mice shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Deliberate physical colocalization can result in quantitatively modest, albeit statistically significant synergistic degradation of polysaccharides during fiber supplementation.
claims.source: These results show that deliberate physical colocalization can result in quantitatively modest, albeit statistically significant synergistic degradation of polysaccharides during fiber supplementation (Supplementary file 5; p<0.05, linear model; diet supplement by bead-type interaction term).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of bead degradation data showing a significant interaction effect.

claims.claim: The specific activity of each isolated arabinan was superior to unfractionated pea fiber.
claims.source: The specific activity of each isolated arabinan (in this case the increase in absolute abundance of the responsive Bacteroides per unit mass of diet ingredient consumed per day) was superior to unfractionated pea fiber (Figure 2C), emphasizing, as others have, the importance of characterizing the effects of plant fibers on both the microbiota and host in order to inform future studies at the intersection of food science, nutrition, and human microbial ecology research (Gidley and Yakubov, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on specific activity calculations shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation to Gidley and Yakubov, 2019.

claims.claim: MFABs represent a technology for measuring biochemical activities expressed by a microbial community of interest in vivo or ex vivo.
claims.source: The bead-based MFABs described in this report represent a technology for measuring biochemical activities expressed by a microbial community of interest in vivo or ex vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the utility of the MFAB technology demonstrated in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A typical gavage of 10^7 beads contained 100 µg of bead-immobilized polysaccharide, 1000 times less polysaccharide than was consumed daily in the diet by mice in the polysaccharide-supplemented arms of the experiments.
claims.source: Determining the latter is challenging in our animal model; a typical gavage of 107 beads contained 100 µg of bead-immobilized polysaccharide, 1000 times more polysaccharide was consumed daily in the diet by mice in the polysaccharide-supplemented arms of our experiments.
claims.evidence: This is based on calculations of polysaccharide amounts on beads versus in the diet.

claims.claim: MFABs possess a greater number of sites for ligand attachment than streptavidin-coated beads.
claims.source: By immobilizing ligand directly on the bead surface, MFABs possess a greater number of sites for ligand attachment than streptavidin-coated beads and include no protein constituents.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of binding sites on both bead types.

claims.claim: Higher ligand density enables higher levels of ligand loading, which reduces the absolute number of beads that need to be administered, recovered, and processed, and increases the dynamic range of a functional activity readout.
claims.source: Higher ligand density enables higher levels of ligand loading, which reduces the absolute number of beads that need to be administered, recovered, and processed, and increases the dynamic range of a functional activity readout.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the higher ligand density of MFABs.

claims.claim: The absolute abundances of B. cellulosilyticus WH2 and Ruminococcaceae sp. TSDC 17.2 increase significantly when animals were consuming the crude pea fiber-supplemented diet, but not during supplementation with either of the isolated arabinans.
claims.source: We found that the absolute abundances of B. cellulosilyticus WH2 and Ruminococcaceae sp. TSDC 17.2 increase significantly when animals were consuming the crude pea fiber-supplemented diet, but not during supplementation with either of the isolated arabinans.
claims.evidence: This is based on community profiling data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The chemistry for covalent polysaccharide attachment to MFABs allows for dense ligand presentation.
claims.source: The chemistry for covalent polysaccharide attachment to MFABs not only allows for dense ligand presentation, but also enables multiple ligands to be simultaneously immobilized to create 'hybrid' beads to model the effects of physical colocalization of different fiber components on microbial degradation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful creation of beads with multiple polysaccharides.

claims.claim: The chemistry for covalent polysaccharide attachment to MFABs enables multiple ligands to be simultaneously immobilized to create 'hybrid' beads.
claims.source: The chemistry for covalent polysaccharide attachment to MFABs not only allows for dense ligand presentation, but also enables multiple ligands to be simultaneously immobilized to create 'hybrid' beads to model the effects of physical colocalization of different fiber components on microbial degradation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful creation of beads with both PFABN and glucomannan.

claims.claim: Crude plant fibers contain various polysaccharides densely intercalated within a cellulose-lignin matrix.
claims.source: Crude plant fibers contain various polysaccharides densely intercalated within a cellulose-lignin matrix (Caffall and Mohnen, 2009).

results.result: An arabinan-containing polysaccharide (PFABN) was isolated from pea fiber using a scalable procedure with 22% yield. The isolated fraction contained 71 mole% arabinose and was characterized as a 2-O-branched arabinan attached to small rhamnogalacturonan-I pectic fragments and galactan oligomers, with approximately 90% of non-starch carbohydrate represented by a single polysaccharide species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C18, C69-C70 provide comprehensive evidence for the isolation and structural characterization of PFABN. The isolation procedure is described in detail with quantified yield (C69-C70), monosaccharide composition is determined by GC-MS (C16), and structural features are defined by glycosyl-linkage analysis (C17). The characterization is thorough and well-documented.

results.result: Sugar beet arabinan (SBABN) is primarily 3-O-branched and structurally distinct from PFABN. PFABN contains twofold more triply branched 2,3,5-substituted arabinose monomers than SBABN, suggesting PFABN is more sterically encumbered.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are supported by glycosyl-linkage analysis data (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1). The structural comparison between PFABN and SBABN is quantitative and based on direct analytical measurements. The inference about steric encumbrance (C21) is reasonable given the structural data.

results.result: In vitro growth assays revealed differential utilization of PFABN and SBABN by Bacteroides species. B. ovatus, B. cellulosilyticus, and B. thetaiotaomicron grew more slowly on arabinans than on glucose, while B. vulgatus grew as rapidly or faster on arabinans compared to glucose.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are supported by in vitro growth curve data (Figure 1C) with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD, FDR corrected). The growth assays provide clear evidence of species-specific differences in arabinan utilization. Sample sizes (quadruplicate cultures) and replication (3 independent experiments) are adequate.

results.result: In gnotobiotic mice colonized with a 14-member bacterial consortium, dietary supplementation with pea fiber, PFABN, or SBABN produced distinct, statistically significant changes in the absolute abundances of specific Bacteroides species. B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482 responded to all three supplements, B. ovatus increased with pea fiber and PFABN but not SBABN, B. vulgatus increased with SBABN, and B. cellulosilyticus and Ruminococcaceae sp. increased only with intact pea fiber.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 are supported by community profiling data from two independent experiments (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2) with appropriate statistical analysis (generalized linear mixed-effects model, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD, FDR corrected, p<0.01). Sample sizes (n=5-6 mice/group, total 10-11 mice/treatment across experiments) are adequate. The use of spike-in bacteria for absolute abundance quantification is methodologically sound.

results.result: Both isolated arabinan preparations (PFABN and SBABN) had significantly greater specific activity compared to intact pea fiber, as measured by the increase in absolute abundance of responsive Bacteroides per unit mass of supplement consumed daily.
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C59 are supported by specific activity calculations (Figure 2C) with appropriate statistical analysis (mixed-effects linear model, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's HSD, FDR corrected, p<0.05). The metric accounts for actual supplement consumption, making it a valid measure of bioactivity. Data from two independent experiments strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Metaproteomic and INSeq analyses identified diet-responsive PULs and fitness-contributing genes in Bacteroides species, providing evidence that PFABN is a key bioactive component of pea fiber utilized by B. thetaiotaomicron, B. vulgatus, B. cellulosilyticus, and B. ovatus.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by gene set enrichment analysis of metaproteomic data (C38, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3) and INSeq analysis (C39, Supplementary file 4), both with appropriate statistical corrections (FDR). The integration of multiple complementary approaches (community profiling, metaproteomics, INSeq) provides strong convergent evidence for C40. However, C40 is an inference that integrates multiple data types.

results.result: Amine plus phosphonate functionalized beads contain 2.18 × 10^10 ± 3.49 × 10^9 reactive amines per bead, representing 23-fold more potential binding sites than streptavidin-coated beads, enabling higher ligand loading on MFABs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 and C62 are supported by quantitative ninhydrin-based colorimetric assay data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and biotin binding site quantification. The comparison between bead types is direct and quantitative. The methodology for amine quantification is established and appropriate.

results.result: In vitro enzyme degradation assays demonstrated that immobilized PFABN on beads is accessible to specific glycosyl hydrolases. A combination of endo-arabinanase and α-l-arabinofuranosidase removed 88 ± 1.2% of immobilized PFABN after 30 minutes, while an endo-inulinase with specificity for β(1-2)-linked fructose failed to degrade PFABN.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by in vitro enzyme degradation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) with appropriate controls (enzyme specificity control with endo-inulinase). The data demonstrate both accessibility of bead-bound polysaccharide and specificity of degradation. Quantification by GC-MS is appropriate.

results.result: In vitro bacterial degradation assays showed that added soluble PFABN was required for degradation of immobilized PFABN from beads by B. thetaiotaomicron and B. cellulosilyticus, with maximum degradation of 64 ± 9% and 48 ± 3%, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by in vitro bacterial degradation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The requirement for soluble PFABN suggests PUL induction is necessary for degradation of bead-bound polysaccharide, which is consistent with the metaproteomic data. However, the mechanism underlying this requirement is not fully explored.

results.result: MFABs recovered from gnotobiotic mice demonstrated that dietary supplementation with pea fiber, PFABN, or SBABN significantly increased microbial degradation of bead-bound arabinans compared to unsupplemented diet. Degradation of PFABN and SBABN was functionally equivalent when diets were supplemented with either isolated arabinan. Xylan was efficiently processed under all supplemented conditions, while galactan was not utilized.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 are supported by GC-MS analysis of monosaccharides remaining on beads recovered from mice (Figure 4B,C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 5) with appropriate statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.05). Germ-free controls (C46) establish bead stability. The functional equivalence claim (C49) is well-supported. Results from cecal and fecal samples were comparable, strengthening conclusions.

results.result: Colocalization of PFABN and glucomannan on the same bead surface resulted in significantly enhanced degradation of glucomannan by the microbiota of mice receiving pea fiber-supplemented diet compared to unsupplemented diet or glucomannan alone. This demonstrates that deliberate physical colocalization can result in statistically significant synergistic degradation of polysaccharides.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 are supported by in vitro growth assays (C53, Figure 5A), prior literature on PUL induction (C54), and in vivo MFAB degradation data (C55-C57, Figure 5D) with appropriate statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test, p<0.05 for C56-C57; linear model with interaction term, p<0.05 for C58). The synergistic effect is modest but statistically significant. The experimental design with hybrid beads is innovative and addresses an important question about fiber structure-function relationships.

results.result: MFABs represent a technology for measuring biochemical activities of microbial communities in vivo. Multiple MFAB types with unique glycan/fluorophore combinations can be simultaneously administered to mice, recovered, and analyzed to directly quantify bacterial metabolism of structurally distinct polysaccharides. The chemistry enables dense ligand presentation and creation of hybrid beads with multiple colocalized polysaccharides.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C60-C61, C63, C65-C66 describe the MFAB technology and its capabilities. The technology is demonstrated throughout the manuscript with successful recovery and analysis of beads from mice. The ability to multiplex different bead types (C3-C4) is shown in Figures 4 and 5. The chemistry for creating hybrid beads (C65-C66) is demonstrated in Figure 5. Claim C61 contains an error (states 1000 times less but text says 1000 times more), but the underlying data about polysaccharide amounts is sound. Claim C63 is a logical inference from higher ligand density.

results.result: The MFAB conjugation chemistry was optimized and characterized. Bead fluorescence could be modulated over four orders of magnitude. Optimal CDAP activation (0.2 mg CDAP/mg polysaccharide) resulted in consistent polysaccharide immobilization. Conjugation levels ranged from 2-20 ng arabinose per 1000 beads for SBABN and 4.43 ± 1.03 ng glucose per 1000 beads for maltodextrin (representing 9.4% of available surface amines).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by optimization experiments and quantitative characterization data (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C). The optimization of CDAP concentration (C72) is well-documented. Quantification of conjugated polysaccharide by GC-MS is appropriate. The range of conjugation levels (C73) reflects variation across multiple experiments, which is expected.

results.result: The MFAB recovery and purification procedure typically recovers 20-50% of input beads from the cecum 4 hours post-gavage, with bead purity after FACS sorting typically exceeding 98%.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 are supported by bead recovery data and flow cytometry analysis. The recovery rate (C76) is reasonable for this type of experiment and is based on data from multiple experiments. The high purity after FACS (C77) is important for accurate quantification of polysaccharide degradation.

results.result: Forward genetic (INSeq) and proteomic analyses were used to characterize the effects of fiber supplements on the bacterial consortium. Bacteroides species possess multiple PULs with conserved features (susC/susD homologs, CAZymes, transcriptional regulators) that enable regulated nutrient acquisition in the competitive gut environment.
results.evaluation: Claim C2 describes the analytical approaches used, which are well-documented in the manuscript. Claims C34-C37 describe established knowledge about PUL structure and function, supported by appropriate citations. The integration of INSeq and metaproteomics is a strength of the study.

results.result: Background and contextual claims about gut microbiota complexity, plant fiber composition, glycan metabolism knowledge, and methodological considerations are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C14, C67-C68, C78-C80 provide background context and are supported by citations to relevant prior literature. These claims establish the rationale for the study and describe established knowledge in the field. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Colocalizing pea-fiber arabinan and glucomannan on the bead surface enhanced in vivo degradation of glucomannan.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is the main conclusion about colocalization effects and is supported by the data in Figure 5D showing significantly more glucomannan degradation when colocalized with PFABN on beads in mice receiving pea fiber-supplemented diet (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U test). This is a key finding of the manuscript.

results.result: β(1-4) galactan degradation in vivo has lower priority compared to available arabinan.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is an inference from the observation that galactan was not utilized under any diet conditions tested (C51). While the data support that galactan was not degraded, the inference about 'priority' is speculative. Alternative explanations (e.g., lack of appropriate enzymes in the community, structural inaccessibility) are not ruled out. The citation to Tuncil et al., 2017 provides some support, but additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish priority.

results.result: B. cellulosilyticus WH2 and Ruminococcaceae sp. TSDC 17.2 increase significantly when animals consume crude pea fiber-supplemented diet, but not during supplementation with either isolated arabinan.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by community profiling data (Figure 2B) and is consistent with C32. This observation suggests these organisms respond to components of pea fiber other than the isolated arabinans, highlighting the complexity of fiber-microbiota interactions.
